title: The beginning (Mark 1:1–8)
hookLine: no birth story, just the beginning of the good news and a voice in the desert

lines: ONE LINE, LIKE A TITLE CARD.
cards: Most stories about a well-known person start with a birth: a baby, a family, a hometown, a childhood. Matthew and Luke do that: angels, shepherds, wise men, a stable. Mark doesn't.
No manger. No star. No Mary and Joseph on the road.
Mark opens with one line, like a title card at the start of a film, then drops you straight into the desert, where a wild man in camel's hair is shouting at crowds.
For forty days, it's Mark start to finish, a few verses at a time. Today's word is in his first sentence: gospel.

teach.b: First, the line. In the Douay-Rheims: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." That's the whole first verse.
Mark says what he's writing and who it's about, and wastes no words. Second, the word.
Gospel comes from old English, god-spel, good story, good news. Mark wrote in Greek, and his word is euangelion.
In his world it was the word for big public news: a victory announced, a new emperor, a royal birth, sent out by messengers to every town.

Greek Isaiah used the same root for heralds running ahead of God, and Paul was already using the word for the message about Jesus. Mark sets it over the whole story: this is the real headline. Third, the voice.

teach.h: A VOICE CRYING IN THE DESERT.
teach.b: Mark quotes the prophets: "A voice of one crying in the desert: Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make straight his paths."
And there's John the Baptist, living rough in camel's hair with a leather belt, eating locusts and wild honey, calling people to be baptized in the Jordan and turn their lives around.

Crowds come from the whole countryside and from Jerusalem. Then John points away from himself: someone mightier is coming after me; I'm not worthy to stoop down and untie his sandals. Fourth, the book.
Mark is the shortest of the four gospels.

teach.h: PREPARE YE THE WAY OF THE LORD.
teach.b: Many scholars think it was the first written, and an early tradition says Mark set down what he'd heard Peter preach. You can read it aloud in about two hours. It moves fast, as tomorrow shows.

how: At Mass, Catholics stand for the Gospel, trace a small cross on forehead, lips and heart as it is announced, and hear it read by a deacon or priest; the Gospel of Mark is read on most Sundays in Year B of the lectionary.

games.q: you're writing the first gospel. you could start with a birth, a family tree, or a childhood. what does Mark do?
o: start with the angels and the manger.
one headline line, then straight to John in the desert.
games.why: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." then straight into the desert.

practice: Find Mark chapter one, verse one, in a Bible or on your phone, or use the words you heard: the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God. Say it out loud, slowly, the way a herald would announce news in a town square.
Then sit with it: what would good news sound like, for you, today? If you pray, you can offer that.

wordCard.voice: Gospel. Old English for good news, from the Greek euangelion, the word for news big enough to send heralds. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: good news, the word used for public announcements, which Mark uses for Jesus.

carryVoice: Your line: gospel means good news. One headline, and the story is off and running. Until tomorrow.
